body:
Apache Iceberg version
1.12.0 (latest release). Also reproduced on 1.10.0. Not reproducible on 1.9.2.
Query engine
Other
Please describe the bug
When expireSnapshots() is used inside a Transaction, the expired manifest lists, manifests and data files are deleted as soon as the transaction-local commit() runs. Nothing has been committed to the catalog at that point. If the process dies, or commitTransaction() fails, the table still references snapshots whose files are gone.
Before 1.10.0 the deletes were deferred. BaseTransaction.expireSnapshots() called expire.deleteWith(enqueueDelete) so the files were only removed by commitTransaction(). #218 added that callback ("keeps track of deletes instead of running them") and #9183 relies on it (the expired files "should be deleted when the transaction commits").
#13631 replaced that method body with appendUpdate(new RemoveSnapshots(transactionOps)). appendUpdate only wires the delete callback for SnapshotUpdate:
// core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/BaseTransaction.java
if (update instanceof SnapshotUpdate) {
  ((SnapshotUpdate) update).deleteWith(enqueueDelete);
}
RemoveSnapshots implements ExpireSnapshots, not SnapshotUpdate, so deleteFunc stays null and RemoveSnapshots.cleanExpiredSnapshots() hands the files straight to FileIO.deleteFile. The existing test testRetainNAvailableSnapshotsWithTransaction only counts files after commitTransaction(), where both behaviours look the same.
Reproduction
Standalone program against the Maven artifacts (HadoopCatalog on local FS, real Parquet rows). TxnExpireRepro.java, build.gradle and run-output.txt are in this gist: https://gist.github.com/namest504/86f80badc49976a4b793f58cb9acd237. Run with ./gradlew run -PicebergVersion=1.12.0 (add the Gradle wrapper or use a local Gradle).
Scenario A, the maintenance job is killed between the two commits:
Transaction txn = table.newTransaction();
txn.updateProperties().set("maintenance.last-run", String.valueOf(cutoff)).commit();
txn.expireSnapshots().expireOlderThan(cutoff).retainLast(1).commit();
// JVM dies here, commitTransaction() never runs
1.12.0 and 1.10.0:
S1 in table metadata:        true
S1 manifest list on disk:    false
read VERSION AS OF S1:       FAILED NotFoundException: Failed to open input stream for file: .../metadata/snap-...avro
read current snapshot:       OK, 200 rows

1.9.2: manifest list still on disk, time travel to S1 returns 100 rows.
Scenario B, another client tags S1 while the transaction is in flight. commitTransaction() fails on re-apply with IllegalArgumentException: Cannot expire ... Still referenced by refs: [audit-2026-10]. The table keeps S1 and the tag, but S1's manifest list is already deleted, so reading the tag fails with the same NotFoundException. On 1.9.2 the tag stays readable.
A unit test shows the difference without any of that setup: after removeSnapshots(tx.table()).expireOlderThan(t).retainLast(1).commit() and before tx.commitTransaction(), the expired manifest lists must still exist and must be in ((BaseTransaction) tx).deletedFiles(). That fails on main and passes with the change below.
Scope
Every release that contains #13631: 1.10.0, 1.10.1, 1.10.2, 1.11.0, 1.12.0 and main. It affects snapshot expiration through the Java Transaction API. The built-in Spark expire action and the Flink maintenance operator call table.expireSnapshots() and do not use that path, but applications running on those engines can.
With file cleanup enabled (the default) the files that go away are the ones the expiration would delete anyway, including manifest lists, unreferenced manifests and data files only reachable from the expired snapshots. The problem is that the catalog metadata still points at them, so time travel, tags, branches and rollback to those snapshots break, and the next expireSnapshots logs NotFoundException retries while reading the missing manifest lists.
Fix
Wire ExpireSnapshots in appendUpdate the same way as SnapshotUpdate:
if (update instanceof Snaps […]
title: Core: `expireSnapshots()` inside a `Transaction` deletes files before `commitTransaction()` since 1.10.0

body:
Apache Iceberg version
1.12.0 (latest release)
Query engine
Other
Please describe the bug 🐞
Summary. With JdbcCatalog, if the database connection drops after PostgreSQL has applied the commit's UPDATE ... SET metadata_location = ? WHERE metadata_location = ? but before the client reads the response, JdbcClientPool (via ClientPoolImpl.run) reconnects and replays the same UPDATE. The replay matches 0 rows because the compare-and-swap predicate no longer holds, so JdbcTableOperations.updateTable throws CommitFailedException for a commit that is already durable. CommitFailedException is a CleanableFailure, so:

with commit.retry.num-retries=0: SnapshotProducer/BaseTransaction run cleanAll() and delete the manifest list and manifests that the table's current metadata now references. The table is left unreadable (NotFoundException on scan).
with the default retries (4), single writer: the Tasks retry refreshes, reuses the staged snapshot id, takes the rollback branch in SnapshotProducer.commit() and returns normally, so it heals by accident.
with the default retries and a concurrent writer committing between the lost acknowledgement and the retry: both commits return normally, but main is rewound to writer 1's snapshot and the other writer's committed data file is no longer visible. Nothing throws.

Verified on Iceberg 1.12.0 against PostgreSQL 17.11 (JDK 21, PgJDBC 42.7.14, InMemoryFileIO), five runs, deterministic. The relevant code is unchanged on main as of 2742348.
Mechanism (1.12.0 sources).

ClientPoolImpl.run(action, retry) re-runs the whole action after reconnect() when isConnectionException(exc) (core/.../ClientPoolImpl.java:69-95). JdbcClientPool passes retryByDefault = true and treats SQLSTATE 08000/08003/08006/08007/40001 as connection exceptions (JdbcClientPool.java:50-51, 110-114). A dropped PostgreSQL socket surfaces as 08006.
JdbcUtil.update(...) runs the CAS UPDATE inside connections.run(...) with that default retry (JdbcUtil.java:533-561). The statement is not idempotent: once applied, a replay updates 0 rows.
JdbcTableOperations.updateTable turns anything other than 1 row into CommitFailedException (JdbcTableOperations.java:146-163) without checking whether newMetadataLocation is already the table's current (or a historical) metadata location.
CommitFailedException implements CleanableFailure; TableOperations.requireStrictCleanup() defaults to true and JDBC does not override it. SnapshotProducer.commit() then calls cleanAll() (SnapshotProducer.java:536-540, 610-616), and BaseTransaction does the same through cleanUp() / cleanAllUpdates() (BaseTransaction.java:380-385, 415-432). Both delete through deleteFile -> the table FileIO.

Other catalogs already reconcile this case: HiveTableOperations (:375), GlueTableOperations (:174), DynamoDbTableOperations and BigQueryTableOperations call checkCommitStatus/checkCommitStatusStrict from BaseMetastoreOperations when the outcome is uncertain. The JDBC table and view operations do not.
Reproduction. A small PostgreSQL-protocol-aware TCP proxy sits between the catalog and the server. Once armed, it forwards the catalog's UPDATE iceberg_tables SET metadata_location ..., withholds every backend message up to and including ReadyForQuery, and closes both sockets. PostgreSQL has committed the row; the client only sees a dropped connection. Full sources (about 350 lines, Gradle project, no object store needed) are in the collapsed section at the end. Run:
docker run -d --name iceberg-repro-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 127.0.0.1:55432:5432 postgres:17-alpine
gradle installDist
build/install/iceberg-repro/bin/iceberg-repro 55432 2>&1 | grep '^RESULT'

Output on stock 1.12.0 (ids vary per run):
RESULT plain_retries_default: responseDropped=true | commit returned normally | table: snapshots=1, current manifest list exists=true, scan OK, data files=1 | deleteFile calls: [snap-429960218544967894-2-b4186a2a-1e7d-40a5-9931-b097c60e6bc4.avro]
RESULT plain_retries_0: responseDropped=true […]
title: JDBC catalog: a dropped connection after the commit UPDATE was applied is replayed by JdbcClientPool, reported as CommitFailedException, and cleanup deletes the committed snapshot's files
AWS: S3FileIO with the default client factory needs the kms and sts SDK modules at runtime; aws.md lists Glue/S3/DynamoDB/KMS/STS

body:
Apache Iceberg version
main (development)
Query engine
Flink
Please describe the bug 🐞
After a table's partition spec changes, Flink upsert and CDC writes can silently fail to update or delete rows written before the change:

An upsert of an existing key leaves both the old and the new version in the table, so the primary key is duplicated.
A CDC delete of such a row has no effect, and the row stays visible.

No error or warning is raised. Compacting the table does not fix it: the stale rows are rewritten as ordinary live rows, and a key is only corrected if it changes again afterwards. This affects v2 and v3 tables with FlinkSink, IcebergSink and DynamicIcebergSink. The spec forbids new equality deletes on v4, but Flink currently still writes them there, so v4 tables are affected too.
Reproduction (v2 table, upsert mode, equality field id):
1. Upsert (1, 'aaa'), (2, 'bbb') into an unpartitioned table.
2. table.updateSpec().addField(bucket("id", 4)).commit()
   -- same as Spark: ALTER TABLE t ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(4, id)
3. Restart the Flink job and upsert (1, 'ccc').
4. SELECT * FROM t
   expected: (1, 'ccc'), (2, 'bbb')
   actual:   (1, 'aaa'), (1, 'ccc'), (2, 'bbb')

The same happens after changing the bucket count, and for CDC deletes of rows written before the change.
DynamicIcebergSink hits this without a manual step, because it evolves the table's spec when records declare a new one. Three variants:

(a) a row upserted under an unpartitioned spec and later, in another checkpoint, under bucket(id, 10) ends up as two identical rows;
(b) the same, but with both writes in one checkpoint;
(c) a writer going back to an earlier spec (bucket(2) → bucket(4) → bucket(2)) leaves the bucket(4) version behind.

Willingness to contribute

 I can contribute a fix for this bug independently
 I would be willing to contribute a fix for this bug with guidance from the Iceberg community
 I cannot contribute a fix for this bug at this time
title: Flink: Upserts and deletes after a partition spec change leave duplicate and deleted rows in the table

It's worse with guarded changes. If both transactions add a snapshot and require main to still be empty (assert-ref-snapshot-id with null), at most one should commit. Both still get a 200, and then one of the snapshots is missing.

Apache Iceberg version
1.10.1 (apache/iceberg-rest-fixture:1.10.1). Also seen with iceberg-core 1.11.0, and the code is the same on main (3ad26de).
Query engine
None (REST API directly)
Please describe the bug 🐞
If a few clients create the same new namespace at the same time, one of them gets a 200 and most of the others get the expected 409, but some get a 500:
UncheckedSQLException: Failed to execute: INSERT INTO iceberg_namespace_properties (catalog_name, namespace, property_key, property_value) VALUES (?,?,?,?)
Caused by: org.sqlite.SQLiteException: [SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY] A PRIMARY KEY constraint failed (UNIQUE constraint failed: iceberg_namespace_properties.catalog_name, iceberg_namespace_properties.namespace, iceberg_namespace_properties.property_key)

The REST spec gives 409: Conflict - The namespace already exists for this case, and that's what a create sent after the first one has finished gets. Nothing is damaged: there's always exactly one winner, and the namespace that ends up stored has only the winner's properties. The problem is just the status. A 500 tells the client it doesn't know whether its create worked, while the catalog actually knows: the namespace exists and this request created nothing.
It isn't specific to SQLite. Gravitino's Iceberg REST server, which uses JdbcCatalog with Postgres, does the same thing:
Caused by: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "iceberg_namespace_properties_pkey"

           public void createNamespace(Namespace namespace, Map<String, String> metadata) {

             if (namespaceExists(namespace)) {

             Map<String, String> createMetadata;

             if (metadata == null || metadata.isEmpty()) {

                   ImmutableMap.<String, String>builder()

                       .putAll(metadata)

Apache Iceberg version
1.12.0 (latest release)
Query engine
Flink
Please describe the bug 🐞
With flink-maintenance.lock.jdbc.init-lock-table=true, two operators in the same job open the same JdbcLockFactory and each tries to create the lock table:

TriggerManager  calls lockFactory.open() in initializeState.
LockRemover calls lockFactory.open() in open() (LockRemover.java:114).

JdbcLockFactory.initializeLockTables()  runs CREATE_LOCK_TABLE_SQL only if the table is missing. That statement is a plain CREATE TABLE without IF NOT EXISTS, so the sequence is check-then-create. If both operators run the
check before either one has created the table, the second CREATE TABLE fails and the task goes to FAILED.
Encountered this bug when writing an E2E test in PR,
#18661 (comment)

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
I've been working on data layout for lakehouse tables on my own, comparing layout strategies head to head on TPC-DS store_sales and NYC taxi data. For Iceberg, what made the biggest difference wasn't the curve itself but how each column gets onto it.
Today zorder(...) and hilbert(...) put each column's full ordered bytes into the key. A long like ss_store_sk (1 to 100) has all-zero leading bytes, while a double like ss_sales_price varies in its sign and exponent bytes. Price takes the high bits, so the rewrite behaves like a sort on price, and queries that filter on the other columns read nearly every file.
In my study, clustering on hand-built 16-bit helper columns (each column scaled linearly to its own range) instead of the raw columns cut store_sales box queries from 0.101 to 0.019 of rows read through Iceberg's reader, and from 164 ms to 85 ms. Asking people to maintain helper columns or run an outside tool isn't a great answer when the rewrite already has what it needs, since file stats carry each column's min and max. So it made more sense to put this in the rewrite itself.
Others have asked for something similar: #5663, and in #3966 RussellSpitzer suggested toOrderedBinary take min/max parameters "so we can shift and tighten the domain". The Javadoc on SparkHilbertFileRewriteRunner.BITS_PER_COLUMN also leaves narrower per-column widths open.
Proposal
An opt-in quantization-bits option for zorder and hilbert rewrites: 0 (default, off), or 8, 16, 24 or 32. When set, each clustered column is mapped linearly from its rewrite group's min and max, taken from file bounds, onto that many bits before interleaving, so every column carries the same weight. There's no extra pass over the data and no spec change. With the option off, output is unchanged.
Results
I measured 16 bits against main on one machine: store_sales at SF10 and NYC yellow taxi 2023, the change backported to Spark 4.1, Iceberg's reader, warm cache, 20 queries per family. Each cell is the median fraction of files scanned / ms.

That depends on the table, so like choosing Z-order or Hilbert in the first place, it's something you'd turn on per table.
Other things I checked:

With the option off, every data file is byte-identical to main's (same sha256 for all files on both tables).
Rewrites with 16 bits ran at 0.72x to 0.83x of main's wall time (median of three builds).
16-bit tables came out 3% to 10% larger at the same target file size.

body:
The REST spec allows multiple storage credentials with different prefixes, but VendedCredentialsProvider.refreshCredential() and OAuth2RefreshCredentialsHandler.refreshAccessToken() require exactly one credential of their storage type. A response with two S3 credentials or two GCS credentials fails with only one S3 credential should exist or only one GCS credential should exist.
This limitation is present at 778d103c0fa802be5e85e4cb2e4e4b4bcd8ac891, the base of #17912. The existing multipleS3Credentials and multipleGcsCredentials tests assert these failures. I also reproduced the AWS failure through AwsClientProperties.credentialsProvider() with a mock endpoint returning two prefix-scoped credentials and initial credentials inside the refresh window.
Refresh should preserve the storage client's prefix and select the applicable credential, without using credentials for an unrelated path. The FileIO-level refresh already retrieves a list; the limitation is in the individual client credential providers.
Found while reviewing #17912. That PR preserves existing provider selection while fixing endpoint resolution; this issue tracks the existing multi-prefix refresh limitation separately. It is distinct from #18817, #18818, and #18819.
title: AWS, GCP: Credential refresh handlers reject multiple credentials of the same storage type

body:
With overwrite(true), DynamicCommitter.replacePartitions adds only the data files of each WriteResult to the ReplacePartitions operation (DynamicCommitter.java#L285-L298). Delete files produced by upserts or CDC deletes are omitted from the overwrite commit without being rejected, which can leave rows visible that those deletes should remove. The Flink docs state that OVERWRITE and UPSERT are mutually exclusive, and IcebergSink and FlinkSink enforce this when the job is built; IcebergCommitter also fails with Cannot overwrite partitions with delete files. The dynamic sink has neither check. The same overwrite commit path exists in Flink 1.20, 2.2 and 2.3.
Reproduction on main at 5b99042b4 (Flink 2.3, TestDynamicIcebergSink style): write the same row four times to an unpartitioned table with upsertMode=true, equality field id, and overwrite(true). In the observed run the job succeeds and reading the table returns 3 identical rows. The final overwrite replaced an earlier one-record data file with a three-record file, so the exact count depends on checkpoint timing. The last snapshot has replace-partitions=true and total-delete-files=0.
Expected: reject overwrite results that contain delete files, as the other sinks do, instead of committing only their data files.
title: Flink: DynamicIcebergSink in overwrite mode silently drops delete files

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
Scan planning on large tables allocates one PartitionData (plus its backing Object[]) per manifest entry, even when millions of files share a small number of distinct partition values. On merge-on-read tables with many small files and many delete files (e.g. after heavy DV/position-delete churn without regular compaction), this produces millions of redundant PartitionData instances on the Spark driver during scan planning and contributes materially to Driver OOM.
Observed evidence (production heap dump, Spark driver)
Table scanned: ~4.4M data files + ~4.34M delete files, only a few thousand distinct physical partitions.

Class
Instance count
Retained

org.apache.iceberg.PartitionData
8,738,866
~489 MB

java.lang.Object[] (backing arrays)
9,697,151
~614 MB

PartitionData count == data files + delete files exactly: each manifest entry pays for a private copy, allocated via BaseFile's copy constructor:
// BaseFile (copy constructor)
this.partitionData = toCopy.partitionData.copy();
PartitionData.copy() / copyFor() unconditionally allocate a fresh instance and backing array; there is no deduplication across entries with identical partition values.
Query engine
Spark
Willingness to contribute

 I can contribute this improvement/fix independently

Proposed approach
Route PartitionData.copy() / copyFor() through a weak Guava Interner so entries with equal partition spec and values collapse to a single shared instance. Weak keys ensure interned instances are evicted once nothing references them, so this is safe for long-lived processes planning scans across many tables.
Two supporting changes:

PartitionData.equals/hashCode currently use Arrays.equals(Object[], Object[]) / Arrays.hashCode(Object[]), which compare elements by reference — partitions with BINARY/FIXED columns (stored as byte[]) never compare equal. Switch to Arrays.deepEquals / Arrays.deepHashCode so binary partition values intern correctly (this is independently a latent correctness bug for any Map/Set keyed on PartitionData with binary partition columns).
Retain Interner/Interners in the minimized relocated bundled-guava jar (GuavaClasses), which currently strips them.

Related work on the same Driver-OOM theme: #18359 (reduces DeleteFileIndex memory for file-scoped position deletes/DVs). This improvement is complementary and addresses a different allocation source.
title: Core: Intern PartitionData during scan planning to avoid duplicate allocations

Apache Iceberg version

Query engine

Problem
Creating a table with a file:///... JDBC catalog warehouse produces mixed URI spellings: the metadata JSON's location uses file:///..., while metadata file paths use file:/....
Both forms are valid local file URIs (RFC 8089), but rewrite_table_path compares prefixes textually. A file:/... source prefix matches file paths but not location; a file:///... prefix has the opposite problem.
Reproduction
Run the attached script with uv and Java installed:
uv run --script repro_file_uri.py
It downloads dependencies, creates a temporary SQLite JDBC catalog with a local file:///... warehouse, creates a table, inserts one row, and calls rewrite_table_path. No metadata is manually modified.
The script exits with:
IllegalArgumentException: Path file:///tmp/iceberg-file-uri-.../warehouse/db/t/
does not start with file:/tmp/iceberg-file-uri-.../warehouse/

Expected behavior
rewrite_table_path should handle equivalent local file URI spellings consistently and relocate a normally created table without manual metadata changes.

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
Problem
We run Spark jobs on Kubernetes (EKS) that authenticate to an Iceberg REST catalog (Databricks Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST endpoint) using workload identity. Each job has a short-lived subject token, the pod's projected service account token, which is exchanged at the catalog's OIDC endpoint (RFC 8693) for a short-lived access token. We want this without distributing a client secret to the job, and with token lifetimes kept short for security reasons.
Existing options don't fit this pattern:

token is a static value. Long-running jobs fail once it expires.
rest.auth.type=oauth2 with credential requires a client ID and secret, which we're trying to avoid.
BearerAuthManager (#18754) reads the token from a file on a fixed reload interval. Iceberg doesn't check token expiry, so refresh timing depends on an external producer writing the file ahead of expiry. Iceberg never calls that producer, and a stale file causes requests to fail.

Requested capability
Let users configure a token provider class that Iceberg calls to obtain a bearer token. Iceberg should own the refresh schedule: refresh a configurable margin before expiresAt, retry on failure while keeping the current token, invalidate and fetch again on a 401, and share one token across sessions and tables in a catalog.
Proposed interface
public interface BearerTokenProvider extends AutoCloseable {
  /** Returns a valid access token and its expiry. Called on startup, before expiry, and after a 401. */
  BearerToken fetchToken() throws IOException;
}

public record BearerToken(String value, Instant expiresAt) {}
Configuration (names are a suggestion):
rest.auth.type=bearer
rest.auth.bearer.token-provider=com.example.TokenExchangeProvider
rest.auth.bearer.token-provider.<key>=<value>   # passed to the provider

Acceptance criteria

Refresh happens before expiresAt minus a configurable margin, not on a fixed interval.
If a refresh fails, the current token stays in use and a retry is scheduled.
A 401 triggers one immediate re-fetch.
One token is shared by all sessions and tables in a catalog.
Provider configuration is passed through, and Iceberg needs no secrets in its own config.
Tests cover refresh timing, retry on failure, and concurrent access.

Use cases

Kubernetes projected service account token exchanged with the catalog's identity provider
Cloud workload identity (AWS, GCP, Azure) exchanged for a catalog access token
Platform-issued federation tokens for any REST catalog that supports token exchange

Related: #18754 (file-based BearerAuthManager), #13550 (original bearer-from-file request)
Environment: Iceberg 1.9+, Spark (version), Scala (version), Kubernetes (EKS)
Contribution: I can contribute a patch if the design is acceptable.

Query engine
Spark

body:
Apache Iceberg version
None
Query engine
None
Please describe the bug 🐞
Bug description
ParquetDictionaryRowGroupFilter may incorrectly exclude row groups when evaluating predicates involving positive and negative floating-point zero.
Apache Iceberg's expression semantics treat -0.0 and +0.0 as equivalent for float and double predicate comparisons. However, the dictionary-filter implementation uses the literal comparator for equality, inequality, and dictionary membership checks.
Because Java's floating-point comparison ordering distinguishes the two signed-zero representations, this can produce incorrect filtering decisions.
Example scenario
Consider a Parquet row group where a dictionary-encoded float or double column contains -0.0.
A query predicate such as:
x = 0.0
should match rows containing -0.0.
However, when the dictionary filter evaluates the predicate using the default comparator, it may conclude that the dictionary does not contain a matching value and incorrectly skip the row group.
Expected behavior

-0.0 and +0.0 should compare as equivalent for Iceberg float and double predicates.
Dictionary filtering must not incorrectly prune row groups containing matching values.
Equality, inequality, range comparisons, and set predicates should follow Iceberg's expression semantics.

Proposed investigation and fix

Inspect signed-zero comparisons in ParquetDictionaryRowGroupFilter, particularly equality, inequality, and range predicates.
Reuse the signed-zero-aware comparison semantics introduced in PR #18813 where appropriate, without adding an unnecessary cross-module dependency.
Add regression tests using dictionary-encoded float and double values, covering both signed-zero directions.
Verify that predicate evaluation never incorrectly excludes a row group containing a matching value.

Related references

Issue #18723 — Signed-zero predicate-evaluation bug.
PR #18813 — API predicate-evaluation fix.
Discussion: #18813 (comment)

CC @Rishavbhattarai — thank you for identifying this additional case and offering to help test the follow-up.
This issue tracks the Parquet dictionary-filter investigation separately so that PR #18813 can remain focused on API predicate-evaluation correctness.

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
TestIcebergSinkTableMaintenance (Flink 1.20, 2.2 and 2.3) has two tests that run a job with a blocking env.execute() and no time limit: testCompactFileE2e and testAllMaintenanceE2e. The MiniCluster in these tests has a single TaskManager. If an earlier test in the same JVM takes that TaskManager down, the job can never be scheduled, and env.execute() blocks until the workflow's 60-minute timeout-minutes cancels the whole CI job.
When that happens:

The job is reported as cancelled, not failed, so the real failure is hard to find.
The upload-artifact step only runs on failure(), so it is skipped and the test reports are lost.
About 40 minutes of runner time are spent waiting on a job that can never run.

This happened several times this week on Flink 2.2 and 2.3. Every one of these jobs shows the same sequence: testConvertEqualityDeletesWithRewriteEnabledE2e passes and cancels its job, both testConvertEqualityDeletesE2e cases fail after their 2-minute Awaitility wait, and then testCompactFileE2e(jdbc) hangs until the CI job is cancelled.

https://github.com/apache/iceberg/actions/runs/42990142430/job/130420727984 (Flink 2.2, Java 21)
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/actions/runs/42994039853/job/130459654426 (Flink 2.2, Java 21)
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/actions/runs/42967832350/job/130349067576 (Flink 2.2, Java 17)
https://github.com/apache/iceberg/actions/runs/42944696901/job/130274568989 (Flink 2.3, Java 17)

The root cause was an exception thrown from DataFileRewriteCommitter.close() while a job was being cancelled. That is addressed by Flink: Always reset commit service after watermark in DataFileRewriteCommitter and its backport Flink: Backport: Always reset commit service after watermark in DataFileRewriteCommitter (#18849). Flink: Make DataFileRewriteCommitter close idempotent fix ci timeout is still open for the case where the job is cancelled before the watermark arrives. This issue is only about making the next hang of this kind fail fast with a clear error.
Proposal
Add a JUnit @Timeout to TestIcebergSinkTableMaintenance in all three Flink versions. TestFlinkIcebergSinkV2 and TestIcebergSinkV2 already do this with a class-level @Timeout(value = 60).
The limit must be longer than the 2-minute Awaitility wait in testConvertEqualityDeletesE2e and testConvertEqualityDeletesWithRewriteEnabledE2e. That means either a class-level limit of a few minutes, or a per-method @Timeout on just the two tests that call env.execute().
An alternative is to replace env.execute() in those two tests with executeAsync() followed by jobClient.getJobExecutionResult().get(timeout, unit).

Flink

body:
Apache Iceberg version
1.11.0
Query engine
Spark
Please describe the bug 🐞
Problem
SparkBatch.planInputPartitions() creates a new table broadcast and a new FileIO broadcast every time it is called:
Broadcast<Table> tableBroadcast =
    sparkContext.broadcast(SerializableTableWithSize.copyOf(table));
Broadcast<FileIO> fileIOBroadcast =
    sparkContext.broadcast(SerializableFileIOWithSize.wrap(fileIO.get()));
SparkScan.toBatch() returns a new SparkBatch on each call, so nothing is reused between calls, even though the table and the FileIO do not change during the lifetime of a scan.
Spark calls planInputPartitions() once per copy of a scan's physical node, while it is still planning the query. When dynamic partition pruning filters nest over a chain of joins on a partition column - something similar to SPARK-48486 - Spark plans an exponential number of copies, and each one adds two broadcasts to the driver. Iceberg never destroys these broadcasts, so they stay in the driver's block manager until the plans that reference them are garbage collected.
What we saw
A production query on Spark 4.1.1 with Iceberg 1.11.0, with 17 left joins of which 10 are on the partition column:

the driver created 264,382 broadcasts, exactly half from each of the two sparkContext.broadcast calls above and none from anywhere else
the driver's MemoryStore went from 14.2 GiB free to about 1 MiB in roughly 6.5 minutes and never recovered
the driver failed without starting a job or a stage

The same query succeeds with spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled=false.
The Spark 3.5, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 modules on main have the same code.
Expected
Planning input partitions again for the same scan should reuse the broadcasts it already created. The number of broadcasts should grow with the number of scans in the query, not with the number of times Spark plans them.
How to reproduce
Create seven small partitioned tables and join them on the partition column, with a selective filter on the first one:
CREATE TABLE t0 (id BIGINT, ds STRING) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (ds);
INSERT INTO t0 VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c'), (4, 'd');
-- repeat for t1 .. t6

SELECT t0.id
FROM t0
LEFT JOIN t1 ON t0.ds = t1.ds AND t0.id = t1.id
LEFT JOIN t2 ON t0.ds = t2.ds AND t0.id = t2.id
LEFT JOIN t3 ON t0.ds = t3.ds AND t0.id = t3.id
LEFT JOIN t4 ON t0.ds = t4.ds AND t0.id = t4.id
LEFT JOIN t5 ON t0.ds = t5.ds AND t0.id = t5.id
LEFT JOIN t6 ON t0.ds = t6.ds AND t0.id = t6.id
WHERE t0.id < 3;
With default settings this query creates 415 to 429 broadcasts on main, depending on the Spark version, for seven tables of four rows each. The count can be read from the Created broadcast N from broadcast at SparkBatch.java lines in the driver log, or from the ID of a broadcast created before and after the query. Each additional join on ds roughly doubles it.
Calling scan.toBatch().planInputPartitions() repeatedly on a single scan shows the same thing in isolation: every call creates two new broadcasts.
Scope
The exponential number of DPP subqueries is a Spark planning problem and is tracked in SPARK-48486 (it is unverified if this spark issue is exactly the nesting root cause) . This issue is only about Iceberg creating new broadcasts for every one of those planning calls, which turns slow planning into a driver out-of-memory failure.
Willingness to contribute

 I can contribute a fix for this bug independently
 I would be willing to contribute a fix for this bug with guidance from the Iceberg community
 I cannot contribute a fix for this bug at this time
title: Spark: SparkBatch broadcasts the table and FileIO on every planInputPartitions call, exhausting driver memory with nested DPP filters

body:
Apache Iceberg version
1.12.0 (latest release)
Query engine
Spark
Please describe the bug 🐞
If the connection fails after a commit request has been sent to a REST catalog (no response, a
connection reset, a read timeout), the Java client reports an ordinary failure:
org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.RESTException: Error occurred while processing POST request
Caused by: org.apache.hc.core5.http.NoHttpResponseException: 127.0.0.1:43911 failed to respond

The server may well have applied the commit. In that case the outcome is unknown, just as for a
5xx response, but the client doesn't say so:

It is not a CommitStateUnknownException, so callers have no warning that the commit may have
landed. An application or scheduler that retries the failed operation writes the data twice.
RESTTableOperations.commit never attempts the reconciliation it already does for 5xx
responses, where it reloads the table and checks whether the snapshot it added is there.

For comparison, the same commit answered with a 504 is reconciled: Spark reports success, with one
copy of the data.
Cause
HTTPClient.execute wraps any IOException in a plain RESTException, so a transport failure
never reaches ErrorHandlers.tableCommitHandler(), which maps 500/502/503/504 on a commit to
CommitStateUnknownException. RESTTableOperations already carries a note about this:
// TODO: ensure that the HTTP client lib passes HTTP client errors to the error handler
RESTSessionCatalog.commitTransaction (multi-table transactions) has the same problem.
To reproduce
With Iceberg's own reference catalog (apache/iceberg-rest-fixture) and a small proxy between Spark
and the catalog that forwards one table commit, lets the catalog apply it, and then closes the
connection instead of relaying the response:
"""Forwards HTTP to a REST catalog. After GET /__arm, the next table commit is
forwarded (so the catalog applies it) but its response is never sent: the
connection is closed instead, as a network failure would."""
import http.client, http.server, re, sys, threading

LISTEN, UPSTREAM = int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2])
armed = threading.Event()
COMMIT = re.compile(r"/namespaces/[^/]+/tables/[^/]+$")
SKIP = {"host", "connection", "content-length", "transfer-encoding"}

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"

    def forward(self):
        if self.path == "/__arm":
            armed.set()
            self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Length", "0"); self.end_headers()
            return
        n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)
        body = self.rfile.read(n) if n else None
        upstream = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", UPSTREAM)
        upstream.request(self.command, self.path, body, {k: v for k, v in self.headers.items() if k.lower() not in SKIP})
        resp = upstream.getresponse()
        data = resp.read()
        if self.command == "POST" and COMMIT.search(self.path.split("?")[0]) and armed.is_set():
            armed.clear()
            print(f"proxy: catalog answered {resp.status} to POST {self.path}; dropping the connection instead", flush=True)
            self.close_connection = True
            return
        self.send_response(resp.status)
        for k, v in resp.getheaders():
            if k.lower() not in SKIP:
                self.send_header(k, v)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        if self.command != "HEAD":
            self.wfile.write(data)

    do_GET = do_POST = do_DELETE = do_HEAD = do_PUT = forward

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", LISTEN), Handler).serve_forever()

python3 proxy.py 18291 8181

body:
Feature Request / Improvement
Background
Apache Iceberg supports different storage systems through its FileIO abstraction. These storage systems may expose the same underlying data through multiple access protocols or filesystem interfaces.
For example, an object storage system may provide access through native filesystem APIs, S3-compatible APIs, or other storage-specific protocols. Different compute engines may prefer different access mechanisms depending on their runtime environment, performance requirements, and available integrations.
Currently, Iceberg file locations are persisted in table metadata and are used by compute engines to access metadata files, manifest lists, manifests, data files, and delete files.
When multiple engines access the same Iceberg table through different storage protocols, differences in URI schemes and filesystem implementations can create interoperability challenges.
One catalog supplies one base location (one scheme). Relative paths resolve against the catalog-provided base; if that base is storage://…, an engine wanting a different physical protocol still needs runtime, engine-side translation.
Existing v1–v3 tables (and absolute paths in v4) keep fully-qualified URIs. Relative paths only help new writes; this FileIO serves the installed base with no metadata rewrite.
Problem Statement
There is a need to decouple the storage location represented in Iceberg metadata from the protocol or filesystem implementation used by a compute engine to access the underlying data.
A consistent, canonical URI representation would allow multiple compute engines to access the same Iceberg table through their preferred storage protocols without requiring protocol-specific locations to be persisted in table metadata.
Without such a mechanism, tables created through one storage access protocol may not be directly accessible to engines configured to use another protocol, even when both protocols address the same underlying storage.
Additionally, Iceberg Format V4 introduces support for relative file paths, where file locations can be stored relative to the table location. This requires URI resolution mechanisms to account for both relative and absolute paths while maintaining consistent storage access across different protocols.
Proposed Solution
Introduce a CanonicalUriFileIO implementation that separates the canonical URI representation persisted in Iceberg metadata from the physical URI used for storage operations.
The implementation should provide a configurable mechanism to resolve canonical URIs into protocol-specific URIs at runtime, based on the storage access configuration of the compute engine.
The proposed implementation should:

Maintain a consistent canonical URI representation in Iceberg table metadata, independent of the underlying storage access protocol.
Resolve canonical URIs to the appropriate physical storage URI at runtime.
Delegate filesystem operations to the configured underlying FileIO implementation.
Apply URI resolution consistently to all file operations performed through this FileIO — manifest lists, manifests, data files, delete files, and metadata files when written/read via this FileIO.
Ensure that newly written file locations preserve the appropriate logical representation (canonical absolute URI or relative path) according to the Iceberg table format version.
Support configurable URI mappings without introducing dependencies on any specific storage system or filesystem implementation.

Example
Consider a storage system that exposes the same underlying data through multiple protocols:
Compute engine	      Canonical URI in Iceberg metadata	     Physical access URI
Engine A	          storage://warehouse/db/table/...	     protocol-a://warehouse/db/table/...
Engine B	          storage://warehouse/db/table/...	     protocol-b://warehouse/db/table/...
Engine C	          storage://warehouse/db/table/...	     protocol-c://warehouse/db/table/...

All engines operate on the same Iceberg tab […]
title: Support Canonical URI Resolution in Iceberg FileIO for Multi-Protocol Storage Access

body:
Apache Iceberg version
1.6.1
Query engine
Spark
Please describe the bug 🐞
Summary
With Spark 3.5.4 or later and the Iceberg 1.6.x Spark 3.5 runtime, Iceberg's vectorized Parquet reader returns wrong values without any error for every row after the first batch (5,000 rows by default) of each data file. Sometimes the executor crashes instead (SIGSEGV, "double free", IncompatibleClassChangeError: vtable stub). Files on disk are correct; only the read is wrong.
This was fixed on main by #11731 (Bump Apache Spark to 3.5.4) and backported to 1.7.x (released in 1.7.2). It was never backported to 1.6.x.
Cause
Spark 3.5.4 (SPARK-50235, SPARK-50463) changed the code generated for ColumnarToRow: it calls ColumnarBatch.closeIfFreeable() after each batch. ColumnVector.closeIfFreeable() calls close() by default; vectors that reuse their memory must override it with a no-op, as Spark's own vectors do.
IcebergArrowColumnVector in 1.6.x reuses its Arrow vectors for every batch of a file but does not override closeIfFreeable(). After the first batch, Spark closes the vectors; Iceberg then writes the next batches into released buffers. Iceberg sets arrow.enable_unsafe_memory_access=true, so there is no bounds check and no error: Spark reads zeros or stale values (e.g. DATE columns become 1970-01-01), and the stray writes can corrupt other memory.
It only happens with whole-stage codegen on (the default), and only when Iceberg uses the vectorized reader (all projected columns are primitive).
Affected versions

Iceberg
Spark 3.5.0 - 3.5.3
Spark 3.5.4+

≤ 1.7.1 (iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.12)
OK
affected

1.7.2, ≥ 1.8.0
OK
OK (fixed by #11731)

Reproduction
Spark 3.5.8 (any 3.5.4+), Java 8, iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.12-1.6.1.jar. One data file of 1,000 rows, read with a batch size of 100:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (
    SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]")
    .config("spark.jars", "iceberg-spark-runtime-3.5_2.12-1.6.1.jar")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.local", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.local.type", "hadoop")
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.local.warehouse", "/tmp/iceberg_repro")
    .getOrCreate()
)

expected = spark.range(0, 1000).selectExpr(
    "id", "date_add(date'2025-01-01', cast(id % 5 AS INT)) AS d", "id * 10 AS v", "concat('row_', id) AS s"
)
expected.coalesce(1).writeTo("local.db.t").tableProperty("write.distribution-mode", "none").create()

actual = spark.read.option("vectorization-enabled", "true").option("batch-size", "100").table("local.db.t")
print(actual.exceptAll(expected).count())
Expected: 0. Actual: 900 on Linux (every row after the first batch); on macOS the JVM crashed with SIGSEGV. With spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage=false, vectorization-enabled=false, or Spark 3.5.3, the result is 0.
We first hit it in production: a table with years() partitions (files > 5,000 rows) came back with wrong dates after a Spark 3.5.1 → 3.5.8 upgrade; smaller days() partitions hid it.
Why a backport to 1.6.x
1.6.1 is the last Iceberg release that runs on Java 8: 1.7.0 and later need Java 11. Spark 3.5.x still supports Java 8, so Java 8 Spark 3.5 users have no fixed release:

upgrading Iceberg to 1.7.2 is not possible on Java 8;
staying on Spark ≤ 3.5.3 means giving up the Spark 3.5.4 - 3.5.8 fixes, including security fixes;
turning off vectorized reads (spark.sql.iceberg.vectorization.enabled=false) works, but costs about 25 - 30% on scans in our tests.

And the failure mode is silent wrong results, which users of 1.6.1 with a recent Spark 3.5 may not have noticed.
The fix is the same 5-line override as in #11731, plus the spark-hive35 bump to 3.5.4 so that 1.6.x is built and tested against a Spark version that has closeIfFreeable(). I have a PR ready against 1.6.x.
I understand that 1.6.x is not actively maintained. Even if a 1.6.2 release is not planned, having the fix on the 1.6.x branch would help Java 8 users who build from it, and this issue documents the incompatibility […]
title: Spark 3.5.4+: vectorized Parquet reads return wrong values in 1.6.x (backport #11731 to 1.6.x)
